reconcile.connective: JFB explains that Luke's general term "apostles" is satisfied by the two individuals Paul names — Peter and James — so history and epistle agree.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman argues Luke's "the apostles" reflects his unity agenda, against Paul's insistence he saw only Peter and James.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: "After Paul Converted... Does the Book of Acts Contradict Paul Himself?", The Bart Ehrman Blog
skeptic.attribution: Bart D. Ehrman, "After Paul Converted... Does the Book of Acts Contradict Paul Himself?" The Bart Ehrman Blog (June 28, 2023)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Compare Act 9:27-28, wherein Luke, as an historian, describes more generally what Paul, the subject of the history, himself details more particularly. The history speaks of "apostles"; and Paul's mention of a second apostle, besides Peter, reconciles the Epistle and the history.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly reconciles Acts' plural 'the apostles' with Galatians' naming of exactly two — Peter and James — as the same visit described at different levels of generality.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), note on Acts 9:27
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this passage directly: the 'apostles' Barnabas brought Saul to are identified as Peter and James specifically, citing Galatians 1:19, and Paul's fifteen-day stay of Galatians 1:18 is folded into the same visit narrated in Acts 9:26-28.
